prompt:
Ultraviolet light of wavelength $250\ \text{nm}$ falls on a metal surface whose work function is $3.2\ \text{eV}$.

**(a)** Calculate the energy of one photon, in eV. **[2]**

**(b)** Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons, in eV. **[1]**

**(c)** State the stopping potential. **[1]**

**(d)** The intensity of the light is doubled at the same wavelength. State and explain the effect on the stopping potential and on the photocurrent. **[2]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $E = \tfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \tfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.00 \times 10^{8}}{250 \times 10^{-9}} = 7.96 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$ ✓ $= 4.97\ \text{eV}$ ✓

**(b)** $E_{k,\max} = 4.97 - 3.2 \approx 1.8\ \text{eV}$ ✓

**(c)** $1.8\ \text{V}$ ✓

**(d)** Stopping potential unchanged because each photon still has the same energy ✓; photocurrent doubles because twice as many photons per second release twice as many electrons ✓

prompt: The work function of a metal is $\Phi$. What is the longest wavelength of light that can release photoelectrons?
An electron and a proton have the same kinetic energy. Which is correct about their de Broglie wavelengths?
markscheme: **B.** $p = \sqrt{2mE_k}$, so the lighter electron has less momentum and a longer $\lambda = h/p$.

prompt:
X-ray photons of wavelength $5.00 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{m}$ are scattered by free electrons.

**(a)** Calculate the wavelength of photons scattered through $120^\circ$. **[2]**

**(b)** Calculate the kinetic energy given to the recoiling electron in this event. **[2]**

**(c)** Explain why this effect cannot be explained by a wave model of light. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $\Delta\lambda = 2.43\times10^{-12}(1 - \cos120^\circ) = 3.65\times10^{-12}\ \text{m}$ ✓; $\lambda_f = 5.37\times10^{-11}\ \text{m}$ ✓

**(b)** $E_k = hc\left(\tfrac{1}{\lambda_i} - \tfrac{1}{\lambda_f}\right)$ ✓ $= 1.989\times10^{-25}\left(\tfrac{1}{5.00\times10^{-11}} - \tfrac{1}{5.37\times10^{-11}}\right) \approx 2.7\times10^{-16}\ \text{J}$ ✓

**(c)** A classical wave would make the electron oscillate and re-emit at the same frequency/wavelength; a change in wavelength requires a particle (photon) collision transferring momentum ✓
